Riverside Medical Centre

22 Riverside Walk, London, SE10 9AB
Dear Dr Anita Kerr
Michael Carter, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: H837294 NHS No. 7845632190
Flat 3, 14 Millstream Court, London, SE10 8PT 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. As you know he has generalised epilepsy. Since my last assessment he reports a variable pattern of episodes but overall a frequency of ≤ four seizures per week, typically brief generalised convulsions or absence episodes as described below. He has maintained good adherence to medication and has been keeping a diary which corroborates this frequency.

He describes two main event types: (1) abrupt loss of awareness with eyelid fluttering and brief behavioural arrest lasting 10–20 seconds, occurring in clusters on stressful days; and (2) generalised tonic–clonic seizures, usually from wakefulness, lasting around 60–90 seconds with post‑ictal fatigue and myalgia. There have been no focal warning symptoms, tongue biting is occasional, and injuries have been minor (one bruised shoulder last month). There is no clear menstrual or sleep‑deprivation trigger; however, he notes that missed meals and high caffeine intake may precipitate events. Family members have witnessed several episodes and confirm generalised onset without lateralising features.

Past antiseizure medication side effects have been documented historically, including a pruritic rash with Lamotrigine (resolved on cessation) and gastrointestinal upset with Valproate (nausea and dyspepsia at higher doses). He is currently taking Levetiracetam 1 g b.d. and Clobazam 10 mg nocte. He reports mild irritability on Levetiracetam that is tolerable and denies current rash, visual disturbance, or significant gastrointestinal symptoms. No recent hospital admissions. He does not drive.

Examination today was unremarkable with normal cognition, intact cranial nerves, and no focal neurological deficits. Weight and metabolic observations are stable. Previous EEG demonstrated generalised spike‑and‑wave discharges consistent with a generalised epilepsy syndrome; MRI brain (last year) was normal.

Plan: We discussed ongoing self‑management and recording of events. Given the present pattern of ≤ four seizures per week and acceptable tolerability, he prefers to continue current therapy for now while we complete repeat EEG with hyperventilation and photic stimulation to re‑assess generalised activity. I have arranged this for the next available slot and requested medication levels and routine bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) to ensure no biochemical contributors. We also reviewed safety, seizure first aid, and avoidance of identified precipitants. He is aware of SUDEP information resources. Follow‑up is planned in 4 months, with earlier review if the frequency increases or new adverse effects occur.

- Follow-up: Telephone review in 4 months or earlier if two or more events occur within a month. Patient will forward seizure diary screenshots monthly via secure portal.

Thank you for your ongoing care and for assisting with prescription continuity while he is overseas. Please contact me if any issues arise.

Combined generalised and focal epilepsy. The patient has both generalised and focal epilepsy, with generalised tonic–clonic seizures occurring from sleep and focal aware auras occasionally progressing to focal impaired awareness events.

Dr Green  
St Thomas' Hospital

Dear Dr Green,  

Michael Turner, DOB: 22-03-1981, Hospital No: H947520 NHS No. 9057314628  
Flat 12, 5 Riverside Walk, London, SE1 9PP 

Diagnoses: 

Generalised epilepsy with prior EEG demonstrating generalised spike-and-wave activity (2017) 

Current Medication: 

Levetiracetam 1 g bd  
Clobazam 10 mg nocte (prn for travel-related sleep disruption) 

Plan: 

- Optimise sleep hygiene around long-haul travel; structured jet‑lag plan provided  
- Adjust Levetiracetam timing to destination time zone within 24–48 hours of arrival  
- Continue current regimen; consider sodium valproate only if inadequate control persists after optimisation and discussion of risks  
- Arrange ambulatory EEG if further breakthrough events occur despite adherence  
- Provide fit note guidance and safety advice regarding driving, swimming, heights, and machinery  
- Telephone follow‑up in 6 weeks, video review in 3 months  

I reviewed Michael Turner via scheduled telephone appointment today, consistent with his frequent business travel pattern across multiple time zones. He reports irregular sleep, prolonged flights, and variable meal schedules, often with overnight work calls. Over the last four weeks he has experienced many convulsions in past month, described as sudden loss of awareness followed by generalised tonic–clonic activity lasting 1–2 minutes with tongue‑bite on one occasion and post‑ictal confusion for up to an hour. These events clustered after eastbound flights and consecutive nights of restricted sleep (3–4 hours). There is no reported alcohol excess; adherence to medication is generally good, though he occasionally takes the evening dose late when transiting. He denies focal auras, focal neurological deficit, or head injury. 

The clinical picture remains in keeping with generalised epilepsy. He previously had an EEG in 2017 showing generalised spike‑and‑wave discharges, and a normal MRI brain. Bloods last month (U&E, LFT, FBC, B12, folate, TSH) were unremarkable. There are no intercurrent infections. 

We discussed practical measures tailored to his travel: bringing a medication schedule card aligned to destination time, setting dual‑time alarms, avoiding red‑eye flights where feasible, and prioritising the first two nights of consolidated sleep. I advised he keeps a rescue plan; clobazam has been helpful around long‑haul trips and can be used cautiously for anticipated sleep deprivation. I also provided written seizure first‑aid for colleagues. 

Driving: he is aware of DVLA guidance; given recent generalised seizures, he should refrain from driving and will seek advice per Group 1 licensing regulations. Safety counsel provided regarding showers (prefer baths avoided or with supervision), working at heights, and operating heavy machinery. 

I have not arranged routine blood monitoring for Levetiracetam. If further convulsions occur despite the above strategies and confirmed adherence, we will discuss alternative agents (notably sodium valproate, acknowledging teratogenicity is not a consideration for him) or adjuncts. Ambulatory EEG may help quantify interictal burden during travel weeks. 

In summary, breakthrough seizures have coincided with disrupted sleep and rapid time‑zone changes; there have been many convulsions in past month. The plan focuses on optimising circadian alignment and dosing timing, with close follow‑up by phone. 

Yours sincerely,

- Patient-reported triggers include sleep deprivation and stress; she will keep a seizure diary to document timing, possible precipitating factors, and any evolution of myoclonic symptoms.  
- Contraception and family planning were discussed in the context of generalised epilepsy and current medication; she plans to review options with primary care and will inform us of any changes.

- Provide written seizure first-aid guidance tailored to the kitchen environment and confirm safe task allocation during peak heat periods.

Consultant Neurologist,

Thank you for your referral. I reviewed Daniel Harris following concerns raised by his employer about recurrent collapse events occurring during shifts in a commercial kitchen. He works the hot line in a high-temperature, fast-paced environment, often during evening service. He attended today with his colleague who has witnessed several recent episodes.

Collateral descriptions are limited by the hectic nature of the kitchen and the lack of continuous observation.

Given the ongoing events arising on most working days and the safety-critical environment (sharp tools, hot oil, open flames), further characterisation is necessary. I have requested urgent ambulatory EEG with concurrent event diary, and I will also arrange a sleep-deprived EEG if the first study is non-diagnostic. Basic bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, glucose, magnesium) and serum antiseizure medication level have been ordered. I have advised the employer and patient that a temporary restriction from high-risk stations is prudent pending assessment, and the patient will discuss adjusted duties with occupational health. We also talked about hydration and structured meal breaks during service, as he reports going long stretches without fluids.

Daniel Harris understands the plan and agrees to keep a detailed log of events, noting timing, context (heat level, task, stress), and recovery period. I will review him in clinic after investigations. Please let me know if there is any additional history from primary care that would assist, particularly previous imaging or prior EEG results.

Riverside Medical Practice

12 Riverbank Way

Dear Dr A. Patel
Michael Turner, DOB: 14-03-1955, Hospital No: H937521 NHS No. 8421905630
Flat 3, 28 Willow Street, London, SE1 3JT 

Diagnoses/summary: History of recurrent unprovoked seizures of uncertain character and cause. Multiple routine EEGs previously nondiagnostic. No clear structural lesion identified on prior brain imaging per patient report.

Prior medication trials (per patient and records): Sodium valproate (sedation and tremor), carbamazepine (skin rash), levetiracetam (irritability), lamotrigine (insufficient benefit), clobazam PRN (helpful for clusters but daytime drowsiness). No history of topiramate, zonisamide, lacosamide, perampanel, or brivaracetam use.

Comorbidities: Mild hypertension (on amlodipine). No known cardiac murmur. No history of head injury or CNS infection. No family history of epilepsy recalled.

I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today. He is a newly retired secondary-school teacher living alone. He reports a predictable daily routine with early mornings, scheduled walks, and reduced social interaction since retirement. He keeps a seizure diary on paper and on his phone. He describes episodes that remain variably stereotyped. He notes that over the course of most calendar cycles he will have several events, sometimes in loose clusters, with longer quiet spells in between. He associates poorer sleep and missed meals with increased likelihood of events. He denies tongue biting or prolonged post-event confusion in every instance, though on occasion he experiences notable fatigue afterwards. There is no clear photic trigger, and he does not drive.

Current medication:
- Amlodipine 5 mg once daily
- Clobazam 10 mg at night PRN for clusters (used sparingly)
- Vitamin D 1000 IU once daily

Examination today was unremarkable. Weight stable. No focal neurological deficits. Blood pressure 138/82. He brought recent home BP readings which are broadly similar. Diary review suggests several events spread across most months, typically brief, with occasional back-to-back occurrences on successive days. No injuries reported.

Investigations and plans:
- Bloods today: FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, vitamin D level, thyroid function.
- Arrange MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) to update prior imaging from several years ago, as records provided were incomplete.
- Discussed treatment options, including introducing a different anti-seizure medicine. He wishes to consider this after reviewing the MRI and bloods. We also discussed safety at home given that he lives alone: kettle use seated, avoiding high ladders, and considering a wearable alert device. He has already placed pans on back hobs and keeps the bathroom door unlocked.
- Agreed to continue clobazam PRN for short clusters only and to maintain a detailed seizure diary noting sleep, meals, and stressors.
- Provided information on local peer support groups; he will explore options that fit his routine to mitigate social isolation.

Follow-up:
- Telephone review by epilepsy nurse in 6–8 weeks to check diary, adherence, and side effects if any changes occur.
- Face-to-face clinic review in 3–4 months or sooner if events increase in intensity, duration, or lead to injury.
- Emergency plan discussed: seek urgent help if an event lasts longer than 5 minutes or if there are repeated events without full recovery.

Thank you for your continued care and support with blood pressure monitoring and general health maintenance. Please let me know if there are any concerns in the interim.

- Provide information on seizure first aid to partner and signpost to patient support resources.

Follow-up: Nurse-led telephone check-in in 6–8 weeks to review ambulatory EEG scheduling and interim events; clinic review in 4 months, earlier if required.

Amelia Thompson is followed in our service for focal epilepsy. She reports that over the past three months she has experienced two drop attacks and five tonic-clonic in the past three months. Current medication:
• Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily.
• Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily.

Her description of brief focal aware episodes (epigastric rising sensation and déjà vu) occasionally progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures is in keeping with focal epilepsy, likely temporal lobe onset. • Arrange MRI brain with epilepsy protocol (3T) and repeat EEG with sleep deprivation to refine localisation.
• Provide written advice on sleep hygiene and seizure triggers; patient will review feasibility of reducing night shifts with her employer.
• Safety counselled regarding drop attacks and convulsive seizures at home and in public; discussed SUDEP awareness and first-aid guidance with her and her partner.
• Driving: she has already informed the DVLA and is not driving.

Examination today: Well-appearing, oriented, normal speech, no focal neurological deficits. Weight stable over the past year. Blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm regular.

Investigations: Repeat serum valproate level to be checked (trough). U&E, LFTs, FBC requested. Consider repeat EEG with sleep deprivation to capture generalised discharges and nocturnal events; ambulatory EEG if scheduling delays.

Plan:
- Generalised epilepsy: Given ongoing nocturnal events and the pattern over the past two months (three focal onset seizures and three focal automatisms in the past two months alongside suspected generalised events), we will prioritise sleep optimisation and adherence. The patient understands this staged approach.
- Safety: Night-time precautions discussed (low bed height, remove sharp furniture edges, partner to use side positioning if safe, consider bed alarm). Buccal midazolam supply to be checked in date. Seizure diary to continue.
- Lifestyle: Advice on regular sleep routine despite shifts; sleep hygiene leaflet provided. Limit alcohol. Encourage vitamin D supplementation and weight maintenance.
- DVLA: Patient is not driving and will continue to follow DVLA regulations for epilepsy.
- Follow-up: Nurse telephone check-in in 6 weeks to review seizure diary, sleep schedule, and blood results. Clinic review in 4 months, earlier if events escalate or injuries occur.

Generalised epilepsy

Diagnosis:

Seizure disorder with ongoing monitoring; current pattern described below.

Aetiology:

No clear structural or metabolic cause identified to date on available records.

Other Medical Problems:

Vitamin D insufficiency under primary care surveillance; intermittent tension-type headaches linked to poor sleep.

Social/Background:

Awaiting relocation from temporary accommodation; reports crowded living conditions with variable night-time noise and disrupted sleep.

The patient reports a longstanding history of brief, sudden collapses without warning, described as drop attacks twice a year. These events are unwitnessed on occasion; when witnessed, there is an abrupt loss of postural tone with rapid recovery and minimal confusion. Investigations:

- Prior MRI brain (report available from 2023) reportedly unremarkable.
- Routine EEG in 2022 non-diagnostic; no definite epileptiform discharges recorded.

Management Plan:

1) Continue Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily and Clobazam 10 mg nocte; maintain a single consistent brand of Lamotrigine.

5) Bloods today: Lamotrigine trough level, FBC, U&Es, LFTs, vitamin D recheck.
6) Review in six months, or sooner if frequency increases or any injury occurs.

He feels generally well between events, remains in employment, and is keen to proceed with further monitoring. He understands the plan and agrees.

Thank you for asking me to review your patient, whom I saw in clinic today, accompanied by her partner and an assistance dog in training provided through a charitable programme. She reports that her habitual events have persisted over the last year and she has begun logging them with a menstrual tracking app to better understand timing. She has previously tried levetiracetam for six months but discontinued due to irritability. No known drug allergies. She uses a period-tracking diary and has begun aligning her logs with her partner’s notes and smartwatch detections of elevated heart rate during events; these data suggest the cyclical clustering described above.

The assistance dog in training remained calm and did not interfere with the assessment; she reports the dog has been conditioned to alert her partner when she becomes unresponsive, which has improved safety at home.

Prior investigations: routine EEG six months ago was within normal limits. MRI brain (1.5T) last year was reported as structurally normal. Bloods including U&E, LFT, glucose, thyroid function and prolactin (post-event sampling not obtained) have been unremarkable. Cycle tracking notes were shown on her phone and suggest the temporal clustering stated above.

- Repeat high-resolution MRI brain (3T) with epilepsy protocol to be arranged.
- Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily for now; she prefers to avoid changes until after the monitoring period. She understands the importance of strict adherence and will continue to log events.
- Safety advice reinforced: avoid baths unsupervised, consider showering with door unlocked, caution with heights and open water, and continue partner supervision during higher-risk days as per her log. The assistance dog training team will be informed (with her consent) of monitoring dates so they can support exposure in a controlled manner.
- I have provided a seizure first aid leaflet and discussed SUDEP risk in simple terms; she is aware of the benefit of regular sleep and stress management.
- We discussed that if the cyclical pattern is consistently demonstrated on monitoring, we could explore time-targeted strategies in liaison with her GP and gynaecology colleagues.

Thank you for asking me to review your patient. I saw him in follow-up today with his partner present. Unfortunately, there has been a clear deterioration in his seizure control over recent months. He works in a cleanroom/data-hall environment with strict access controls. He reports that retrieval of rescue medication and arranging timely refills are often significantly delayed due to site procedures, and he has consequently missed doses on several occasions. He describes more frequent events, with clusters occurring up to 7 in bad weeks, and shorter inter-seizure intervals compared with earlier this year.

He has a history consistent with combined generalised and focal epilepsy. He and his partner report two main semiologies: (1) episodes beginning with a rising epigastric sensation, brief behavioural arrest, rightward head turn and lip-smacking lasting 30–60 seconds, followed by several minutes of confusion; and (2) generalised convulsive seizures without warning, with bilateral tonic–clonic activity, tongue biting and myalgia after recovery. Nocturnal events have been noted on two occasions this month by wearable alert, and there has been one daytime convulsion at work necessitating first-aid support. Post-ictal recovery is taking longer (30–90 minutes) than previously. There are no consistent triggers other than the missed/late medication doses related to workplace access constraints.

He reports strict adherence when able to access his medication, and he carries written confirmation from Occupational Health outlining his need for rapid access to anti-seizure medicines; however, he states that on multiple shifts he was unable to leave the controlled area promptly, resulting in delayed dosing. He has reduced confidence at work and has avoided overtime due to fear of clusters. There is no current alcohol or recreational drug use, and sleep is suboptimal on rotating shifts.

Examination today was non-focal. Cardiovascular observations were normal and there were no interictal neurological deficits. There were no features to suggest an acute intercurrent illness. Review of previous investigations confirms a diagnosis of combined generalised and focal epilepsy: prior EEGs demonstrated generalised spike–wave discharges and independent left temporal sharp waves; MRI brain (2023) showed no structural lesion.

Current treatment: Levetiracetam 1.5 g twice daily; Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily; rescue Midazolam buccal 10 mg as needed for prolonged seizures. He reports that the rescue medication is stored off-floor and requires supervisor release, leading to delays. Pharmacy refills are reportedly postponed when he is on long shifts, contributing to missed evening doses.

In summary, this is a patient with combined generalised and focal epilepsy who is experiencing a worsening trajectory of seizure control, with clusters up to 7 in bad weeks, temporally associated with delayed access to regular and rescue medication within a high-security workplace. While his baseline regimen has previously been effective, the emerging pattern and functional impact indicate deterioration driven by real-world barriers to timely dosing. We discussed strategies to mitigate risk and he will continue to document events, missed/late doses, and work-related access delays in a seizure diary. He understands SUDEP information previously provided and continues to use nocturnal alerts as tolerated. I will liaise with Occupational Health to provide an updated medical letter detailing the necessity for immediate access to prescribed antiseizure medication and rescue therapy during all shifts.

I will review him again in six weeks or sooner if there are further clusters or injuries.

- Diagnosis status: under review for seizure disorder; classification not specified at present.

- Reported seizure frequency: sz *six/mo, described by the primary carer as brief episodes with post-event tiredness.

- Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily: mood and irritability monitored; carer reports mild fluctuations but no major behavioural change.

Dr A. Malik
Riverside Health Centre

12 Stonebridge Way
Southwark
London SE1 5JT
Dear Dr A. Malik
Jordan Ellis, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: H927451 NHS No. 8439201756
Flat 3, 28 Wharf Street, London SE8 4DN 

Diagnoses/summary: Recurrent unprovoked seizures with ongoing events; prior routine EEG reported as non-diagnostic; brain MRI (2023) structurally normal; ongoing occupational risk due to warehouse duties between tall racking and narrow aisles

Previous medication: Levetiracetam (behavioural irritability), Lamotrigine (rash after titration), Carbamazepine (dizziness), Sodium valproate (weight gain, tremor), Lacosamide (no clear benefit), Clobazam PRN (sedation)

Not taken: Topiramate, Zonisamide, Perampanel, Brivaracetam, Rufinamide, Pregabalin, Tiagabine

Occupational context: Works as a warehouse picker in narrow aisles between tall racking; shift patterns vary with differing lifting demands and pace. Reports that rushing during late shifts increases stress and poor sleep. Has used a voice-activated headset for picking which is sometimes disorientating during post-event confusion.

I reviewed Jordan Ellis in clinic today. They attended alone. They report ongoing brief losses of awareness with sudden behavioural arrest and occasional falls. Frequency currently described as "sz x3/d" on their seizure diary, with clustering on late shifts. They note pre-event sensations of light-headedness, ringing in the ears, and a rising nausea on some days, but at other times events occur without warning. Post-event fatigue lasts 20–40 minutes. No tongue-biting or urinary incontinence reported recently. A witness at work described staring, dropping the handheld scanner, and a slow return to baseline. No clear alcohol excess; caffeine 2–3 cups/day. Sleep fragmented on rotating shifts.

Investigations: Routine EEG (2024) non-diagnostic; no interictal epileptiform activity captured. MRI brain (2023) reported no focal cortical abnormalities. Bloods (Aug 2025): FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT within reference range; vitamin D low–normal. No known head injury. No family history of epilepsy reported.

Current medication:
- Brivaracetam 50 mg twice daily (initiated by prior team; modest reduction in duration but not frequency)
- Folic acid 5 mg daily (precautionary)
- Omeprazole 20 mg daily (dyspepsia)

Adverse effects: Reports occasional low mood and reduced motivation since starting brivaracetam; denies suicidality. No visual symptoms or rash.

Functional/safety considerations: Given the warehouse role between tall racking and narrow aisles, we discussed immediate safety measures: stepping away from elevated pallets when feeling unwell, informing a supervisor of ongoing events, and avoiding climbing or working at height. They do not operate forklifts. Has a personal alarm badge but not consistently used.

Plan:
- Continue brivaracetam 50 mg twice daily for now. I have provided written information and discussed potential titration options at follow-up depending on tolerability and effect.
- Arrange ambulatory EEG (48–72 hours) aiming to capture typical events, timed across two shift patterns if possible.
- Repeat bloods including vitamin D and brivaracetam level (baseline) before any dose change.
- Seizure diary to continue; patient to record shift type, sleep duration, and any missed meals alongside event times to correlate with "sz x3/d" entries.
- Occupational advice letter (separate) to employer recommending avoidance of tasks at height and working alone in narrow aisles until better control is achieved; encourage buddy system during late shifts.
- Lifestyle measures discussed: sleep regularity where feasible, hydration, and pacing during high-demand shifts; patient to trial pre-shift snack to mitigate light-headedness.
- DVLA guidance reiterated; patient confirms they are not driving.
- Follow-up in 8–10 weeks, sooner if deterioration or adverse effects. If ambulatory EEG captures typical events, we will review therapeutic options including alternative agents not yet tried.

Thank you for your ongoing care and prescription support. Please let me know if you or the patient have any concerns before the next appointment.

Thank you for asking me to review this gentleman. I met him in clinic today accompanied by his partner. He reports episodic events going back many years. The typical spell, as described by his partner, begins with a brief disengagement and guttural vocalisation, followed by rhythmic rocking of the trunk while unresponsive; he subsequently appears confused and fatigued, with recovery over approximately 45–60 minutes. He does not recall most of the episode. There have been rare events during sleep where she has noticed similar rocking and a short cry, with him being difficult to rouse afterwards. He also describes separate episodes where he becomes very tearful and overwhelmed without loss of awareness; these were volunteered as distinct from the episodes outlined above.

In terms of timing, they currently cluster such that he tends to experience a spell roughly once in a fortnight—he phrased it as happening about every second week—though there can be longer quiet intervals followed by two close together. He feels this interval has been broadly stable over the past year.

He cycles to work most days and states he prefers this for routine and fitness; he has not noticed any consistent relationship between commuting days and the occurrence of events. Sleep has been variable due to workload, and he occasionally wakes unrefreshed.

Past medications have included levetiracetam (mood irritability), carbamazepine (dizziness), and topiramate (word-finding difficulty). Currently he is taking brivaracetam 100 mg twice daily and lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily, which he reports are generally well tolerated. He has had no drug allergies.

Neurological examination today was unremarkable. Mood appeared tense but coherent, with no thought disorder elicited. There is a prior history of a brief post-event confusional state requiring short observation in 2023, but no recent behavioural disturbance.

Given the longstanding history and the present description, I would like to obtain prolonged video-EEG monitoring with sleep capture to better characterise these events, and I have discussed this with him and his partner. He is agreeable. I have also requested updated MRI brain (3T) with epilepsy-focused protocol. Bloods arranged today include FBC, U&E, LFT, vitamin D, and trough levels for lamotrigine and brivaracetam for reference. We will review results and consider rationalisation of therapy depending on the monitoring outcome.

I will keep you informed of progress. Please let me know if there are any interim concerns from your side.

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Focal epilepsy with probable temporal lobe onset


Present Medication:

1. Lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily

2) Adjust levetiracetam to 500 mg twice daily to even out peak–trough variability and reduce evening clustering of focal events. The patient has previously tolerated this dose without mood disturbance.
3) Non-pharmacological measures (patient-reported goals): partner-assisted night feeds where possible, scheduled daytime nap when support available, and consistent wind-down routine before 21:30 to reduce sleep-onset latency.
4) Safety counselling reinforced: avoid co-sleeping when drowsy, continue seizure precautions at changing table and bath time, and do not sleep on elevated surfaces with the infant.
5) Arrange an ambulatory EEG if events persist beyond eight weeks despite dose adjustment, to confirm focal onset. If seizures remain frequent, we will consider introducing lacosamide as adjunctive therapy or rationalising levetiracetam depending on tolerance.

Dear Dr Jonathan Hale
Alex Morgan, DOB: 14-03-1987, Hospital No: H927451 NHS No. 8427193056
Flat 3, 28 Willow Road, London NW3 1TR

Diagnoses/summary: Drug-resistant focal epilepsy, likely temporal lobe origin. Photosensitivity to flicker and bright light reported. Prior EEGs and video-EEG have demonstrated frequent focal discharges. Electrographic seizures frequent on EEG (~6/h).

MRI brain (2018): No definite focal cortical dysplasia or hippocampal sclerosis identified. Subtle asymmetry of the left hippocampus noted without signal change (radiology felt non-diagnostic).

Previous anti-seizure medications: carbamazepine (partial response, dizziness), levetiracetam (mood irritability), valproate (weight gain, tremor), lamotrigine (rash at higher dose), lacosamide (nausea), clobazam PRN (sedation), perampanel (behavioural change), zonisamide (poor appetite), topiramate (word-finding difficulty), gabapentin (ineffective).

Not previously tried: brivaracetam, cenobamate, eslicarbazepine, pregabalin, rufinamide, tiagabine, oxcarbazepine.

Comorbidities: Migraine without aura; mild generalised anxiety (patient-reported). No known cardiac history. Routine bloods last month within normal limits.

I reviewed Alex Morgan in clinic today. They attended alone. They described focal aware episodes with epigastric rising sensation and brief speech arrest, lasting 20–40 seconds, sometimes progressing to impaired awareness with automatisms. Triggers include flickering lights in supermarkets, sunlight through trees while travelling in a car, and certain video content. They have been avoiding known triggers where possible and now use tinted lenses outdoors. Sleep deprivation also appears to lower their threshold.

Since the last review, they report variable days with clusters, particularly late afternoon. A recent ambulatory EEG performed via our service recorded frequent focal discharges over the left temporal region with evolution in rhythm and morphology consistent with electrographic seizures frequent on EEG (~6/h). The patient noted subtle subjective correlates with only a proportion of these events, aligning with under-recognised subclinical activity.

Current medication:
- Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily (maintained due to prior rash at higher dose)
- Clobazam 10 mg nocte PRN up to four nights/week
- Riboflavin 400 mg daily (self-initiated for migraine)

Allergies/adverse reactions: lamotrigine rash at ≥150 mg BD previously; levetiracetam-related mood change.

Plan:
- We discussed therapeutic options including optimisation with brivaracetam or eslicarbazepine, and the possibility of cenobamate in future if standard options fail. We also discussed non-pharmacological strategies given photosensitivity (continued trigger avoidance, screen settings with reduced brightness/blue light filters, and steady ambient lighting). The patient prefers to consider medication changes after a further discussion with family.
- I have arranged an epilepsy nurse specialist telephone review in 4–6 weeks to revisit adding brivaracetam, and to reinforce safety advice around photosensitive triggers. Seizure diary to continue, noting lighting context and sleep pattern.
- We will request repeat MRI with epilepsy protocol given persistent focal features and frequent electrographic seizures, and will discuss at the next MDT for potential surgical candidacy if imaging or semiology evolves.
- Driving: We reiterated DVLA guidance relevant to ongoing focal seizures; the patient verbalised understanding.

Follow-up: Routine clinic in 3 months, sooner if deterioration or if they wish to proceed earlier with medication change.

Flat 3, 28 Willow Street, London EC2A 4BH 

Diagnoses/summary: History of recurrent seizures of unclassified pattern; currently stable. Post-partum within the last six months with fragmented night-time sleep reported. No known structural brain lesion documented to date.

Previous investigations: Routine EEG (2019) reportedly non-specific; no recent neuroimaging available on record.

Current medication: Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily. Folic acid 5 mg once daily (continued post-partum as per patient preference). Vitamin D 1000 IU once daily (over the counter, patient-reported).

Drug history relevant to seizures: Previously tried levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily (discontinued in 2020 due to mood change and irritability). No history of topiramate, zonisamide, or valproate use. No known drug allergies.

I reviewed Amelia Turner in clinic today. She attended with her partner and their infant. She is within six months post-partum and reports fragmented night-time sleep due to infant care, with daytime fatigue. Despite sleep disruption, she remains Free of seizures for 2 year. She last recalled a possible brief aura-like episode over two years ago without progression to a convulsive or impaired awareness event. She does not drive.

She reports good adherence to lamotrigine with no new adverse effects (no rash, no diplopia, no imbalance). Breastfeeding has recently reduced to once nightly; she notes no change in wellbeing. Mood is stable; no red flags for post-partum depression. No intercurrent illnesses, no head injury, no alcohol or recreational drug use. Periods have recommenced and are regular. - General: well-appearing, afebrile, no cardiorespiratory distress.
- Neurological: normal higher functions in clinic conversation, cranial nerves intact, normal tone/power/reflexes, normal gait.

- We discussed that sleep fragmentation can lower seizure threshold; she will continue practical sleep-conservation strategies where feasible and enlist partner support for night feeds when possible.
- Contraception discussed in general terms; she is considering a progesterone-only option via GP. She understands to inform us before any medication changes.

Plan:
1) Continue lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily without change. No dose escalation indicated while she remains Free of seizures for 2 year and tolerating treatment.
2) Sleep hygiene advice reiterated; patient to pace daytime activity and request shared night-time infant care when feasible.
3) Arrange routine serum lamotrigine level only if there are clinical concerns or if a future dose adjustment is contemplated; not required at present.
4) No immediate need for repeat EEG or MRI given current stability; will reconsider if any breakthrough events occur.
5) Pre-conception counselling to be offered if planning pregnancy; continue folic acid as she prefers for now.
6) Follow-up: routine review in 9–12 months, sooner if any suspected breakthrough events, new neurological symptoms, medication side effects, or pregnancy planning.

Currently under review (no specific classification assigned)
